cards.headline: The night the opera house wheeled out the wrong piano
cards.snippet: Jarrett had specified an Imperial Bösendorfer, a near-ten-foot, eight-octave concert grand. What the opera house produced instead was a Bösendorfer baby grand kept for rehearsals — one that wasn't in tune, with pedals that stuck and some keys that didn't work. A replacement Imperial was sourced, but the piano tuner forbade wheeling it across town in rainy conditions and instead set to work making the baby grand playable. “The piano tuner saved our lives,” said Brandes.
cards.context: MOJO's making-of, drawing on Brandes's 2011 BBC account of the afternoon of 24 January 1975.

cards.headline: Why the audience laughs in Part I's first seconds
cards.snippet: A few seconds into Part I, the audience laughs. The story goes that Jarrett opened by quoting the opera house's signal bell — G D C G A D, the notes that call patrons to their seats. Die Welt later disputed it: the house never used that pattern, the paper argued, and the notes may instead be the end of “The Faithful Hussar,” played by the chiming clock of the nearby Haus 4711. Jarrett says he doesn't remember doing it consciously, but credits it with putting the audience in a good mood that helped him through the night.
cards.context: Wikipedia album article, Background section; the Die Welt counter-theory is carried alongside, per the contested-detail rule.

cards.headline: The broken-piano legend, retold by a listener
cards.snippet: …When he came to Koln, the piano that was on stage was the wrong one. It was out of tune, it was half-tail, and the pedals were broken. The man tried to adapt to what he had and was improvising for most of the time. He is a genius!
cards.context: The pool's most-liked eligible comment, on the official Topic upload — a retelling of the wrong-piano story rather than a personal response.

cards.headline: He kept wearing it out, format after format
cards.snippet: Heard it first in 1975 ( I was 13 then). Ruptured the tape cassette... got another one.. and then another. When at last I was able, bought the LP, And when it was no longer audible bought another; recorded it on tape cassettes so I wouldn't spend time without it…
cards.context: The comment runs on past the excerpt: two CDs followed, one scratched by his young son — who now has a master's degree in piano. On the Natella upload.

cards.headline: The Berklee-era dancer
cards.snippet: I was just coming to Boston to dance with a modern company when Jarrett was leaving Berklee School. Our company musicians' hair was on fire from the impact of Keith Jarrett's brief time there. This 'album', along with Belonging and Solo Concerts inspired much of our choreography…
cards.context: She is 74 now, with neuropathy in her legs, and ends the comment: she still can't help but dance to it as best she can. On the Natella upload.

cards.headline: Trzciński plays it from the score — in 31 minutes
cards.snippet: Tomasz Trzciński plays Part I from Jarrett's published transcription, recorded live in Ingelheim in November 2009 for his “Around The Köln Concert” project. His reading runs 31 minutes against Jarrett's 26. One listener: "I'm learning this transcription too, so I understand how challenging this really is."
cards.context: Uploaded to the performer's own channel, Tomasz Trzcinski (Piano Explorations Live!).

version.versionLabel: Keith Jarrett: The Köln Concert - Part I, Tomasz Trzcinski - piano

cards.headline: Bad Timing (1980) gives Part I four and a half minutes
cards.snippet: Part I plays under three sequences in Nicolas Roeg's Bad Timing; the longest, four and a half minutes around the 75-minute mark, scores the confrontation between Milena and Alex. Roeg met Jarrett in person to clear the music.
cards.context: Documented by Everything Jazz's survey of jazz moments in cinema; the film's Wikipedia music listing also credits “The Koln Concert”.
